title: All the rage: clothes and fashion
subtitle: dress codes, chic, off the cuff
summary: Talk precisely about clothes - what to wear at work, how to describe a garment, how to say something is fashionable - and use the many English metaphors built out of clothing words.

lesson.heading: Dressing for work
lesson.text: Students often look **scruffy** in T-shirts and jeans, but people entering the world of business have to learn the **dress code** of the workplace. Business **attire** (a formal word for clothing) needs to project a professional image.

examples.text: Clothing that **reveals** too much of your back, your chest or your **midriff** is not appropriate, even in a casual business setting.
examples.note: reveal = show; the midriff is the part of the body between the chest and the waist

examples.text: **See-through** fabrics should be avoided, and skirts should not be too tight or too short - though nobody wants to look **frumpy** either.
Women often need a good choice of **outfits**, and men find a good range of **suits**, ties and casual jackets **invaluable**.
examples.note: an outfit is a set of clothes for a particular occasion; invaluable = extremely useful

lesson.heading: Workplace clothing vocabulary
rows: untidy (a *scruff* is a person who dresses in an untidy way)
the accepted way of dressing in a particular social group
extra items added to clothing, e.g. jewellery, shoes, cufflinks
decorative objects used to fasten the cuffs on men's shirts
a day, often Friday, when staff can wear more casual clothes
a piece of clothing worn over other clothes to protect them at work
a hat worn to protect the head

lesson.heading: Describing clothes
rows: informal but clean, tidy and stylish

lesson.heading: Buying and wearing clothes
lesson.text: To be **dolled up**, **dressed up** or **done up to the nines** is to be dressed in a very fashionable or very formal way. Where the clothes come from matters too.

examples.text: Some people choose to buy **designer (label)** clothes, but most prefer to buy more cheaply on the **High Street**.
examples.note: the High Street = ordinary, much less expensive shops

examples.text: People who can afford it sometimes have clothes **made-to-measure**, but more often people buy **off the peg**.
examples.note: made-to-measure = made especially for them; off the peg (or off the rack) = ready-made
suit someone = look good on them

lesson.heading: Being in fashion
lesson.text: English has a whole family of expressions for saying that something is fashionable right now - and for the people who follow those fashions.

examples.text: These jackets are **all the rage**. Dresses like this are the **height of fashion**.
The woman was dressed in the **very latest fashion**, and the magazine has **up-to-the-minute** fashion articles.
examples.note: up-to-the-minute = dealing with the most recent trends

examples.text: The film has **set a new trend** for the silk top the star wore. A **trend-setter** is a person whose style is followed by others.
High heels are **on trend** this year, and large handbags are this year's **must-have** item.
examples.note: a must-have item is a thing everyone wants

examples.text: If a fashion **catches on**, it becomes popular. A **slave to fashion** is someone strongly influenced by fashion.
examples.note: slave to fashion is used disapprovingly

lesson.heading: Clothes in metaphors
rows: to be **hand in glove** with someone
to have a close working relationship with them
spending as little money as possible
to have a secret plan or idea

lesson.heading: More clothes metaphors: literal and figurative
rows: make the strap round your waist tighter
start living in a more economical way
a hem is the sewn edge of a garment
a seam joins two pieces of material
to cloak is to cover with a cloak
an achievement to be proud of

lesson.text: *Invaluable* does not mean 'without value' - it means extremely valuable or extremely useful. The real opposite of *valuable* is *valueless*.

exercises.prompt: Match each clothes metaphor with its meaning.

pairs.left: to be hand in glove with someone
pairs.right: to work very closely with them

pairs.left: to do something on a shoestring
pairs.right: to spend as little as possible

pairs.left: to draw a veil over something
to have something up your sleeve
to put someone in a straitjacket

exercises.prompt: Wow, you're done up to ___! Where on earth are you going?
exercises.explanation: Done up to the nines = dressed in a very fashionable or very formal way.

exercises.prompt: The sign outside the bar said: 'Dress code: ___ - no jeans or trainers.'
exercises.explanation: Smart-casual clothes are informal but clean, tidy and stylish.

exercises.prompt: I'm surprised to see girls wearing such ___ dresses in this cold weather.
exercises.explanation: Skimpy clothes are short and use very little material - not warm. (Revealing would also work here.)

exercises.prompt: I can't afford ___ clothes - the labels are far too expensive for me.
exercises.explanation: Designer (label) clothes carry the name of a famous fashion designer.

exercises.prompt: I buy most of my outfits on the ___, in ordinary shops that anyone can afford.
exercises.explanation: Buying on the High Street means buying from ordinary, much less expensive shops.

exercises.prompt: A woman says she finds a particular jacket 'invaluable'. What does she mean?
exercises.explanation: Invaluable means extremely valuable or useful; the opposite of valuable is valueless.

exercises.prompt: Lucy is always dressed in the ___ of fashion - she always looks so chic!
exercises.explanation: The height of fashion = extremely fashionable, like all the rage.

exercises.prompt: As soon as Amy gets home from work, she changes from her smart suit into tracksuit bottoms and a comfortable, ___, old jumper.
exercises.explanation: Baggy clothes are loose and comfortable - the opposite of clingy.

exercises.prompt: These bracelets were last year's ___ item - everybody wanted one.
exercises.explanation: A must-have item is the thing everyone wants that season.

exercises.prompt: Would each of these be appropriate or inappropriate for a job interview?

exercises.statement: If a new fashion catches on, it becomes popular.
exercises.explanation: Correct - catch on means become popular or widely accepted.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite: 'I'm no good at speaking if I haven't had time to prepare.'
exercises.answer: I'm no good at speaking off the cuff.
exercises.explanation: To speak off the cuff is to speak without having prepared anything.
